rationale: Twitter's ToS explicitly states 'you own your Content' and clearly labels platform access as a revocable license, providing more clarity than typical digital goods ToS. However, aggressive unilateral termination rights ('for any or no reason'), extreme liability caps ($100 maximum), and broad sublicensing grants create substantial consumer protection gaps. The document's length and legal complexity substantially obscure these unfavorable terms.
evidence_quotes: you grant us a worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free license (with the right to sublicense) to use, copy, reproduce, process, adapt, modify, publish, transmit, display and distribute such Content
We may suspend or terminate your accounts or cease providing you with all or part of the Services at any time for any or no reason
IN NO EVENT SHALL THE AGGREGATE LIABILITY OF THE TWITTER ENTITIES EXCEED THE GREATER OF ONE HUNDRED U.S. DOLLARS
we may stop (permanently or temporarily) providing the Services (or any features within the Services) to you or to users generally...without prior notice
